newsitem.title: USA: HP paints rosy portrait of future - analysts.
newsitem.headline: HP paints rosy portrait of future - analysts.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co executives presented a generally positive outlook to analysts on Wednesday, describing recent actions to address shortcomings and to prepare for future growth, analysts said.
However, analysts said the company faces difficult comparisons between results in the first half of this fiscal year and strong year-earlier business.
Participants in the semi-annual analyst meeting, held behind closed doors at HP's Palo Alto headquarters, also said the dollar's recent strength could crimp overseas sales revenue.

Hewlett-Packard shares ended up in Wednesday trading, rising 1-1/4 to close at 56-1/8 on the New York Stock Exchange, and hitting 56-3/8 on other U.S. markets after the New York close, up 1-3/4 from its composite close on Tuesday.

In the meeting, executives said July and August had been slow, followed by a strong October, but they cautioned not to over-interpret the shift and declined to discuss trends since the 1997 new fiscal year started November 1.

Analysts praised HP chief executive Lewis Platt for spelling out specific changes the company had made to address underperforming areas, including the decision to shut down its loss-making disk-storage business over the summer.

The company also won kudos for redeploying 75 percent of its employees from the closed operation to other positions in HP and for acting with similar speed to revise inventory and channel management and hone costs.
"The bottom line is positive," said Robert Herwick, president of Herwick Capital Managment. "I think some of the near-term problems have been addressed and addressed effectively."

Analysts said the company's operating margins, which were 8.7 percent in the last quarter of fiscal 1996, are still in recovery mode despite management's statement last month that it aims for 10 to 12 percent levels in the current quarter.

Wall Street estimates of earnings-per-share (EPS) are not expected to change much from their current levels, with First Call consensus estimates flat at $0.75 a share for the first quarter and $3 a share for all of fiscal 1997, analysts said.
HP posted a fiscal 1996 EPS of $2.46, up from $2.31 a year earlier.
Analysts said the company seemed confident that it had moved beyond the price cuts and overstocking of the sales pipeline which had bloated printer inventories in early summer.
The Internet also may help boost sales of printers and printer products, as more documents are sent electronically and printed locally, analysts added.
On the workstation front, executives acknowledged the move to a new generation of high-performance machines was taking longer than had been expected, but are moving to resolve the matter.

Chicago Corp analyst David Wu said executives also spelled out how the move to 64-bit systems will begin in 1997 with software so the move to the Merced microprocessor it is jointly developing with Intel Corp at the end of the decade will not require a shift to new software at that time.
J.P. Morgan analyst Daniel Kunstler said the order outlook in the personal computer sector was positive, and extremely positive for PC servers.
